The Court of Appeal in Abuja has reserved judgment in two related appeals arising from the N100m defamation suit instituted against the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project and others by two operatives of the Department of State Services. The appeals, marked CA/ABJ/CV/1114/2026 and CA/ABJ/CV/1105/2026, challenge the May 5, 2026 judgment of the High Court of the Federal Capital Territory, which awarded N100m in damages against SERAP over publications concerning an alleged visit by DSS operatives to the organisation’s Abuja office in September 2024. The presiding judge, Justice Danlami Senchi, reserved judgment in the appeals on Monday after counsel for the parties adopted their respective briefs of argument. In the appeal filed by Kolawole Oluwadare against Sarah John and two others, counsel for the appellant, O. Adesioye, informed the court that all the briefs of argument had been filed and that the appellant had a pending application seeking an extension of time to appeal and an order deeming the appeal as properly filed. The application, filed on October 22, 2026, was not opposed by counsel for the respondents. Consequently, Justice Senchi granted the application and deemed the appellant’s brief, the respondents’ briefs and the appellant’s reply briefs as properly filed. Adesioye subsequently adopted the appellant’s brief of argument and reply brief, urging the court to allow the appeal against the decision of the FCT High Court. However, counsel for the first and second respondents, O.S. Kehinde, adopted their brief of argument and urged the court to dismiss the appeal. Counsel for the third respondent, Paul Mgbeoma, also adopted his client’s brief of argument. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. In the second appeal, marked CA/ABJ/CV/1114/2026, the Incorporated Trustees of SERAP are challenging the same judgment of the FCT High Court. Counsel for SERAP, Paul Mgbeoma, informed the court that the appeal was ripe for hearing and drew its attention to a pending application for stay of execution, urging that it abide by the outcome of the appeal. He told the court that the notice of appeal was filed on July 27, 2026, while the records of appeal and additional records were transmitted on July 31 and August 13, respectively. Mgbeoma adopted SERAP’s brief of argument, filed on September 4, 2026, and its reply brief, filed on October 8, 2026, urging the court to allow the appeal. But Kehinde, counsel for the first and second respondents, adopted their brief of argument, filed on September 22, 2026, and urged the court to dismiss SERAP’s appeal in its entirety. Justice Senchi subsequently reserved judgment in both appeals for dates to be communicated to the parties. The dispute arose from publications by SERAP concerning an alleged visit by DSS operatives to its Abuja office in September 2024. In its judgment delivered on May 5, 2026, the FCT High Court, presided over by Justice Yusuf Halilu, awarded N100m in damages against the organisation in favour of two DSS officers. SERAP subsequently approached the Court of Appeal, raising 24 grounds of appeal to challenge the decision. In its brief of argument dated the 3rd of September 2026, and filed at the Court of Appeal by SERAP’s counsel, the group raised questions concerning the essential elements of defamation, the evidential burden of establishing identification, the competence of the evidence relied upon by the trial court, and the protection of freedom of expression and public-interest advocacy. “The central issue in this appeal is whether the respondents established by credible evidence that the publications complained of referred to them. The publications did not name the respondents, and the descriptions relied upon were general physical descriptions which did not, without more, identify the particular individuals who brought the action. “The alleged suspension of the 1st and 2nd Respondents was likewise not supported by independent documentary evidence. The award against SERAP was therefore not only excessive but also arbitrary and ought to be set aside. “The learned trial judge relied, inter alia, on assertions that the publication had affected the 1st and 2nd Respondents ‘mentally and psychologically’ and had ‘gone viral’, without sufficient evidence establishing the extent of the publication or any specific professional, financial or reputational injury suffered by the Respondents,” the document read. The appellants further argued that the award of liability could not stand where the essential findings on falsity and justification were not supported by the evidence. “We respectfully submit that the finding of liability and consequential award of damages cannot stand once the findings upon which they were founded are shown to be erroneous. “Where a claimant is not expressly named in a publication, the burden remains on the claimant to establish by evidence the circumstances from which a reasonable reader would understand the publication to refer specifically to that claimant. That essential link was not established in this case,” SERAP stated. The group said the suit instituted by the 1st and 2nd respondents was “frivolous, vexatious and lacked merit given that the publications in question, as shown in Exhibit D2, were made against the SSS as an institution, yet the two unidentified 1st and 2nd Respondents filed this suit in their personal capacities.” They therefore urged the court to set aside the judgment of the FCT High Court as well as consequential orders challenged in the appeal.
